title: DPs & STARs: The On-Ramps and Off-Ramps
hook: The airway system has on-ramps and off-ramps. Here's how to merge.

scenes.narration: Last one for now, kid. Departure procedures and STARs — how you get on the highway, and how you get off without missing your exit.

Departures come in two flavors. O D Ps — obstacle departure procedures — exist purely to keep you off the rocks, no clearance needed. SIDs simplify the clearance AND organize the flow; those, ATC assigns.

Unless the plate says otherwise, departures assume you cross the end of the runway at thirty-five feet and climb at least two hundred feet per nautical mile. That's feet per MILE, not per minute — do the groundspeed math.

STARs are the arrival version — published routes that funnel everyone downhill in an orderly line. Key phrase: 'descend via' means fly the STAR's altitudes yourself. 'Descend and maintain' means fly ATC's number. Don't freelance between the two.
O D P for rocks, SID for flow, two hundred feet per mile unless published otherwise, and know whether you're descending VIA or descending AND maintaining. Merge like you've done it before, kid.
Instrument Procedures Handbook, chapters one and three. Free P D F. Costs only your evening.

quiz.question: The primary purpose of an ODP is:
quiz.explanation: ODPs exist solely for obstruction clearance and may be flown without an ATC clearance; SIDs add flow management and are assigned.

quiz.question: Unless otherwise published, an IFR departure procedure assumes a minimum climb of:
quiz.explanation: The standard is crossing the departure end at 35 ft and climbing 200 ft/NM — a gradient, not a rate. Convert using groundspeed.

quiz.question: Cleared to "descend via" a STAR, you should:
choices: Comply with the published altitude (and speed) restrictions on the chart
Descend to the lowest chart altitude immediately
Wait for a hard altitude from ATC
quiz.explanation: "Descend via" delegates the vertical profile to you — fly the STAR's published restrictions without further instruction.
